concept.name: Instrumental variable
concept.definition: A variable used to identify a causal effect when the regressor of interest is endogenous: a valid instrument is correlated with the endogenous regressor (relevance) and affects the outcome only through that regressor (exclusion restriction), isolating an exogenous source of variation.
concept.intuition: Find a lever that shifts the troublesome variable for reasons unrelated to everything else in the error term, then measure how the outcome responds to those lever-induced shifts only.
concept.mechanics: In two-stage least squares the endogenous x is regressed on the instrument z (first stage) and y on the fitted x (second stage); the just-identified IV estimand is Cov(y,z)/Cov(x,z), interpretable under monotonicity as a local average treatment effect (Angrist, Imbens and Rubin 1996). First-stage F-statistics check relevance; overidentification tests partially probe exclusion.
concept.formula: beta_IV = (Z'X)^{-1} Z'y; in the single-instrument, single-regressor case, beta_IV = Cov(z, y) / Cov(z, x).
concept.failure_modes: Weak instruments (low first-stage F) leave the estimator biased toward OLS with non-normal finite-sample distributions, and the exclusion restriction is untestable in the just-identified case, so invalid instruments deliver consistent estimates of the wrong quantity.
concept.misconceptions: That any variable correlated with x works as an instrument: without a defensible exclusion restriction the estimate is meaningless, and the estimand is local (LATE), not a universal average effect.
concept.example: Angrist used the Vietnam-era draft lottery as an instrument for military service: lottery numbers shifted service probability essentially randomly, identifying the causal effect of service on later earnings.
